name: glossary.json
content:
The names and terms that recur across the chapters, as the book defines them.

Acts of the Apostles
The fifth book of the New Testament, written by the author of the Gospel of Luke. It tells the story of the early church and of Paul's missions, and it is the main source for his life outside his own letters. On several points it differs from them. See [paulus_link slug="the-three-accounts-compared" /].
Antioch
A city in Syria, the early center of the mission that included Paul and Barnabas, where the disciples were first called Christians.
Apostle to the Gentiles
Paul's title for himself (Romans 11:13), claiming the mission to non-Jews as his own. See also Paul the Apostle.
Atonement
The Christian teaching that the death of Christ pays for human sin. ʿĪsā ibn Maryam called people to repentance and obedience to God; Paul made the cross the means of forgiveness. See [paulus_link slug="suffering-that-atones" /] and The Invalidity of the Crucifixion of Jesus as an Atonement of Sin.
Barnabas
An early preacher faithful to the tawḥīd and law taught by ʿĪsā ibn Maryam, who parted from Paul after their conflict over the law of Mūsā and circumcision.
Case against Paul
The argument of this site and the book: six counts, drawn from Paul's own letters and from the record of the first community, that he departed from the teaching of ʿĪsā ibn Maryam. See [paulus_link slug="the-measure" /].
Christology
The branch of Christian theology concerned with the nature and role of Christ. Paul was the first to teach a Christology of absolute divinity.
Cilicia
The Roman province in the south-east of Asia Minor where Tarsus, Paul's birthplace, stood. He preached there after his call.
Corinth
The Greek port city where Paul spent a year and a half (Acts 18:11) and to which he wrote two of his letters.
Corinthians
Two letters of Paul to the church at Corinth. They are the fullest record of his quarrels with a congregation and of what he claims for himself. See [paulus_link slug="the-fruit-at-corinth" /].
Damascus
The city in al-Shām (present-day Syria) near which Saul claimed to have received the revelation that made him a follower of ʿĪsā ibn Maryam.
Death of Paul
The end of Paul's life. The New Testament does not record it; later tradition places his execution at Rome under Nero. See [paulus_link slug="a-death-the-scriptures-never-record" /].
Early Christianity
The faith of the first generations after ʿĪsā ibn Maryam, from the Jewish community in Jerusalem to the churches of the Greek cities. The case asks whether the churches Paul founded kept what the first community held.
Early Islam
The first generations of Muslims and the scholars who recorded what they said. Their reports about Paul are gathered under the Islamic tradition. See [paulus_link slug="the-early-islamic-record" /].
Ephesus
The chief city of Roman Asia, where Paul stayed about two years (Acts 19:10) and wrote to the Corinthians.
False apostle
One who claims an apostleship he was not given. The charge rests on Revelation 2:2, which commends a church for testing those who say they are apostles and are not, and on the doubts about Paul's own claim that he records in 1 Corinthians 9:2. See [paulus_link slug="them-which-say-they-are-apostles" /].
False prophet
One who speaks in the name of God what God has not said. Deuteronomy 13 and 18 give the tests, and the case applies them to Paul. See [paulus_link slug="the-failed-prophet" /].
Fiṭrah
The original, pure state in which human beings are created, inclined toward the truth and the oneness of God. In Islam it is the natural human instinct to know and worship the One God. People depart from it through outside influence such as misguided teaching or upbringing.
Founder of Christianity
The title some scholars give Paul, because the doctrines that mark the church, the divinity of Christ, atonement by the cross and faith without the law, appear first in his letters. See [paulus_link slug="paul-the-father-of-a-new-religion" /].
Galatians
Paul's letter to the churches of Galatia, written in anger over the law and circumcision. It holds his own account of the clash with Peter at Antioch (Galatians 2:11-14). See [paulus_link slug="the-parting-with-barnabas" /].
Gamaliel
The leading Jewish rabbi who taught Paul in Jerusalem in his youth.
Gentile
From the Latin for the nations: anyone who is not a Jew. Here it refers mainly to the Greco-Roman population that Paul targeted.
Gospels
The four accounts of the life of ʿĪsā ibn Maryam in the New Testament: Matthew, Mark, Luke and John. All of them were written after Paul's first letters. They are distinct from the Injīl.
Ḥawāriyyūn
(الحواريون) The faithful disciples of ʿĪsā al-Masīḥ, who continued his mission after he was raised to the heavens.
Hellenism
The influence of Greek culture and philosophy that spread through the Middle East after the conquests of Alexander the Great.
Injīl
The original revelation sent down by God to ʿĪsā ibn Maryam. It is distinct from the books called gospels in Christianity today. See The Authentic Gospel of Jesus.
ʿĪsā al-Masīḥ
A prophet of God from the Children of Israel who brought the teaching of tawḥīd and upheld the law of the Torah. Islam rejects the claims that he was the son of God and that he founded Christianity.
Islam and Christianity
The two faiths as they meet in this case. Islam holds that ʿĪsā ibn Maryam was a prophet and a messenger who taught tawḥīd; the church, as Paul and his heirs shaped it, holds him to be divine. See [paulus_link slug="islamic-dilemma" /].
Islam and Paul
The record of what Muslim scholars have said of Paul, from the first centuries to today: that he turned the message of ʿĪsā ibn Maryam away from tawḥīd. See [paulus_link slug="paul-in-the-islamic-tradition" /].
Islamic tradition
The reports, commentaries and histories of the Muslim scholars, as distinct from the Qurʾān itself. See [paulus_link slug="the-early-islamic-record" /].
Jerusalem Council
The early meeting of the disciples that decided whether Gentile converts had to keep the law of the Torah.
Jesus of Nazareth
The name by which ʿĪsā ibn Maryam is known in the Christian tradition. In Islam he is a prophet and messenger of God.
Justification by faith
Paul's teaching that a person is made right with God through faith in Christ and not through works of the law (Romans 3:28). The letter of James answers it (James 2:24). See [paulus_link slug="justification-by-faith" /].
Letters of Paul
The thirteen letters in the New Testament that carry Paul's name. Seven are accepted as his by nearly all scholars, and six are disputed. See [paulus_link slug="the-letters-of-a-man" /].
Logos
(Λόγος) A concept in Greek philosophy and in the writings of Philo of Alexandria: an intermediary between God and creation. It shaped early Christian theology.
Marcion
A shipowner's son from Sinope who came to Rome about 140. He made a canon of an edited Luke and ten letters of Paul, and rejected the Hebrew Bible. The church condemned him. See [paulus_link slug="paul-and-the-new-testament" /].
Muslim scholars
The commentators, theologians and historians of Islam who wrote about Paul, among them Ibn Ḥazm, al-Thaʿlabī, al-Shahrastānī, al-Kairanawī and Shabbir Akhtar. See [paulus_link slug="modern-voices-from-al-kairanawi-to-akhtar" /].
New covenant
The promise of Jeremiah 31:31-33 that God would write his law on the heart. Paul read it as the end of the old covenant of law; the case reads it as the same law kept from within. See [paulus_link slug="the-gospels-and-the-new-covenant" /].
New Testament
The twenty-seven books Christians add to the Hebrew Bible: four Gospels, Acts, twenty-one letters and Revelation. Thirteen of the letters carry Paul's name.
New Testament canon
The list of books the church accepted as scripture. It settled over several centuries, and thirteen of its twenty-seven books are letters in Paul's name. See [paulus_link slug="paul-and-the-new-testament" /].
Old Testament
The Christian name for the Hebrew scriptures, in an order and with a reading that differ from the Tanakh. Paul quotes it mostly from its Greek translation, the Septuagint.
Original sin
The Christian belief that all people bear guilt for the sin of Ādam. Islam rejects it. See Original Sin Or Original Forgiveness: Which Demonstrates God's Love For The World?
Pastoral epistles
First and Second Timothy and Titus, letters in Paul's name on the order of the church. Most scholars date them after his death. See [paulus_link slug="the-letters-of-a-man" /].
Paul (Saul of Tarsus)
A Jew of Tarsus who claimed to have received revelation and to be an apostle, and who then altered the teaching of ʿĪsā ibn Maryam to win over Gentiles.
Paul and Apollos
Apollos was a Jew of Alexandria and a teacher at Corinth (Acts 18:24; 1 Corinthians 3:4-6), whose following there rivalled Paul's. See [paulus_link slug="paul-and-apollos" /].
Paul and James
James, the brother of ʿĪsā ibn Maryam, led the Jerusalem community. Paul met him (Galatians 1:19), and the two stood on opposite sides of the question of the law (Acts 21:20-25). See [paulus_link slug="james-the-brother" /].
Paul and Jesus
What the sources say of any meeting between them. Paul does not claim to have known ʿĪsā before his death; he claims a later vision (1 Corinthians 15:8). See [paulus_link slug="did-paul-ever-meet-jesus" /].
Paul and slavery
Paul told slaves to obey their masters in letters that carry his name (Ephesians 6:5; Colossians 3:22), and he sent the runaway Onesimus back to Philemon. See [paulus_link slug="paul-onesimus-and-slavery" /].
Paul and the body
The case sets Paul's suspicion of the flesh (Romans 7:18) against the Jewish view of the body and of marriage as good, and traces the first to Greek thought. See [paulus_link slug="the-greek-body-and-the-jewish-bed" /].
Paul and the Tanakh
Paul's use of the Hebrew scriptures, which he quotes mostly from the Greek translation and often reads against their plain sense. See [paulus_link slug="twisting-the-scriptures" /].
Paul and women
What Paul wrote of women, from the silence commanded in 1 Corinthians 14:34 to the co-workers he greeted in Romans 16: Phoebe, Prisca and Junia. See [paulus_link slug="women-paul-greeted" /].
Paul in Acts
The Paul of Luke's second book, a missionary and speaker who keeps the law. He differs in several points from the Paul of the letters. See [paulus_link slug="dale-b-martin-notes-published" /].
Paul in prison
Paul's imprisonments at Philippi, Caesarea and Rome (Acts 16; 23-26; 28). Several letters carry his name from prison. See [paulus_link slug="paul-in-prison" /].
Paul in Rome
The last place where Acts leaves Paul: under guard for two years in his own rented house (Acts 28:30). Acts does not report his death. See [paulus_link slug="did-paul-reach-spain" /].
Paul the Apostle
The name the church gives Paul after his call, also written Saint Paul or St Paul. In his own letters he calls himself an apostle of Jesus Christ and the apostle of the Gentiles.
Paul's character
The portrait of the man in his own letters: his oaths, his curses and his quarrels. See [paulus_link slug="the-character-of-paul" /].
Paul's conversion
The event on the road to Damascus, which Paul calls a revelation (Galatians 1:12) and which Acts tells three times. See [paulus_link slug="the-damascus-road" /].
Paul's psychology
Attempts by scholars to read the man from his words: the persecutor's guilt, the visions and the thorn. See [paulus_link slug="a-psychological-portrait-of-paul" /].
Pauline interpretation
Paul's way of reading scripture, and the church's way of reading Paul. Second Peter 3:16 already says that his letters hold things hard to understand, which the unlearned twist. See [paulus_link slug="twisting-the-scriptures" /].
Paulinism
The system of belief built on Paul's letters, also called Pauline Christianity, or Paulism by its critics. The case on this site is that it is not the religion taught by ʿĪsā ibn Maryam.
Peter (Cephas)
One of the leading disciples of ʿĪsā ibn Maryam, who held to the law of the Torah.
Pharisees
A Jewish party that stressed strict observance of the Torah and the oral tradition; the ideological opponents of the Sadducees. Paul was a Pharisee.
Philo of Alexandria
A Hellenistic Jewish thinker known for joining Platonic philosophy to the Torah. His idea of the Logos is thought to have influenced early Christian theology.
Qurʾān
The final revelation of Islam, in Arabic. It names ʿĪsā ibn Maryam as a messenger and does not name Paul. See [paulus_link slug="the-quran-as-witness" /].
Resurrection
The Christian teaching that Christ rose bodily after the crucifixion. Paul's list of witnesses in 1 Corinthians 15:3-8 is the earliest written account, and it differs from the Gospels. The Qurʾān denies that ʿĪsā ibn Maryam was crucified (4:157). See [paulus_link slug="revelation-or-borrowing" /].
Roman citizenship
Paul's claim, made in Acts only, to be a Roman citizen by birth (Acts 22:28). His own letters never mention it. See [paulus_link slug="the-citizenship-and-the-appeal-to-caesar" /].
Roman Empire
The state in which Paul preached and which made the church its official religion in 380. See [paulus_link slug="what-the-romans-saw" /].
Romans
Paul's longest letter, to a church he had not founded. It holds his fullest statements on justification by faith (Romans 3-5) and on the law (Romans 7).
Sadducees
A conservative Jewish party that rejected the oral tradition and accepted only the written Torah.
Saul of Tarsus
Paul's Hebrew name, Shaʾul, the name he bore as a Pharisee and persecutor before his call. Acts uses it until Cyprus (Acts 13:9) and Paul after.
Second coming
The return of Christ, which Paul expected within his own lifetime (1 Thessalonians 4:15-17). It did not come. See [paulus_link slug="the-failed-prophet" /].
Stephen
The first martyr of the Jerusalem community, stoned with the approval of Saul before his conversion.
Tafsīr
Commentary on the Qurʾān. Some classical commentators on Yā Sīn (36:13-14) name Paul among the messengers sent to Antioch. See [paulus_link slug="pauls-own-titles" /].
Talmud
The compiled body of Jewish oral tradition. Some of Paul's teaching appears to draw on the interpretations it records.
Tanakh
The Jewish name for the Hebrew Bible: Torah (law), Nevi'im (prophets) and Ketuvim (writings). See [paulus_link slug="the-tanakh-rewritten" /].
Tarsus
Paul's birthplace, in Cilicia in Anatolia (modern Türkiye), a center of Greco-Roman learning.
Tawḥīd
(توحيد) Belief in the oneness of God, the foundation of the teaching of every prophet including ʿĪsā ibn Maryam. Paul altered it into a mixed conception of divinity.
Thorn in the flesh
Paul's phrase (2 Corinthians 12:7) for an affliction he asked God three times to remove. Its nature is unknown. See [paulus_link slug="pauls-thorn-in-the-flesh" /].
Torah
The scripture revealed to Mūsā, containing the law binding on the Children of Israel.
Transvaluation
The reversal of a teaching into its opposite while its name is kept: here, Paul's turning of the ethic of ʿĪsā ibn Maryam, the law kept from the heart, into a dogma of salvation by the cross. See [paulus_link slug="the-measure" /].
Trinity
The Christian doctrine that God is three in one: Father, Son and Holy Spirit. It contradicts the original teaching of ʿĪsā ibn Maryam. See Ice, Water and Vapour: The Trinitarian Analogy and the Problem of Rank.
Typology
A symbolic method of interpretation that treats figures and events of the Hebrew Bible as foreshadowings of Christian events. Paul was the first to use it to support his claims about Christ.
Urgemeinde
German for "original community": the first followers of ʿĪsā ibn Maryam in Jerusalem, who held to tawḥīd and the law of the Torah.
Yā Sīn
The thirty-sixth sura of the Qurʾān. Its story of messengers sent to a city (36:13-32) is connected by the commentators with Antioch. See [paulus_link slug="pauls-own-titles" /].
